Overview

 

Building flexibility into domestic energy use is a key element of the UK’s transition to a decarbonised energy system. Researchers in the Faculty of Engineering at the University of Sheffield are working in close collaboration with industrial partners to explore methods to unlock the flexibility inherent in electric storage heating systems. These systems, which are installed in around 1.4 million UK homes, have the potential to make a significant contribution to ambitious, near-term consumer led flexibility targets. 

 

The project – named FairFlexHeat - will develop and trial an integrated approach that makes existing storage heaters work better for customers while enabling consumer-led flexibility. It combines Connected Response’s proven smart controls with dwelling-level physics-informed machine learning, rolling-horizon optimisation, and “home as a battery” state-of-charge estimation approaches being developed at Sheffield. The system will forecast thermal needs and dynamically schedule storage-heater and hot-water charging against weather, prices and grid signals, while maintaining customers’ comfort. Portfolio-level coordination will manage charging across buildings, feeders and substations, supporting demand turn-up, peak reduction and local network flexibility.

 

These technologies aim to address both grid-level and end-user challenges. The approach enables households to benefit novel type-of-use tariffs to be developed within the project, helping reduce both energy bills and carbon footprints. Predictive control systems allow for efficient operation without user input, making these solutions more accessible and user-friendly. We are seeking a researcher with expertise in mechanical engineering or a related subject to play a leading role in delivery of this project, alongside an experienced supervisory team.

 

 

Main duties and responsibilities

Develop and test algorithms for physics-informed machine learning; rolling horizon optimisation; and state of charge estimation for domestic dwellings featuring electric storage heating systems.
Take a leading role in planning and conducting a programme of experimental work to characterise the performance of electric storage heating devices in order to refine system models.
Manage data collection and storage on a day-to-day basis; conduct quantitative analysis and visualisation of experimental data and modelling outcomes.
Take an active role in externally facing engagement and dissemination activities including conference presentations, technology demonstrations, and stakeholder site visits.
Contribute to academic publications and stakeholder-facing reports on the key project outputs.
Attend internal, partner and funder project meeting; contribute to quarterly Monitoring Officer reports.
Carry out other duties, commensurate with the grade and remit of the post.

 Postdoctoral Research Associate in Efficient Algorithms for Multi-Modal Language-Action Models

 Northeastern University London

 Location:  London, Devon House (St Katherines Dock)

 Term:  1 year, fixed term, full-time

 Reports to:  Professor Osvaldo Simeone

 Benefits:  The university supports staff maintaining a good work-life balance, offering: ( i ) flexible working and parental leave opportunities; ( ii ) an employee assistance programme which provides free, confidential advice on both home and work concerns, as well as optional private medical insurance; ( iii ) season ticket loans; and ( iv ) being part of the cycle-to-work scheme.

 Start:  February-March 2027

 The Role   

 Northeastern University London invites applications for a Post-Doctoral Research Associate in Efficient Algorithms for Multi-Modal Language-Action Models , working with Professor Osvaldo Simeone and Professor Bipin Rajendran. The position is funded through an ARIA grant focused on democratizing AI through brain-inspired, energy-efficient approaches to training and adaptation. 

 The successful candidate will join a research team working to develop theoretically principled, energy-efficient, and reliability-aware frameworks for next-generation AI, with a particular emphasis on the fine-tuning and efficient implementation of language models, vision-language-action models, and world-action models. Key application areas include edge intelligence, low-power autonomous systems, and communication networks. 

 The candidate will contribute to research on:

 Developing novel algorithms and theoretical frameworks for parameter-efficient and energy-efficient multi-modal language-action models, with an emphasis on reliability, scalability, and resource-constrained settings.

 Designing, implementing, and experimentally evaluating AI models and fine-tuning methods, including developing reproducible software pipelines, benchmarking computational and energy efficiency, and analysing performance across language, vision, and action-based tasks.

 Publishing research findings in leading journals and conferences in machine learning, information theory, and quantum information.

 Presenting research findings at project meetings, workshops, and international symposia.

 Supporting the supervision and mentoring of PhD students and research assistants within the group.

 Contributing to the preparation of project deliverables, technical reports, and future funding proposals.

 We particularly encourage applications from candidates belonging to groups underrepresented in UK higher education. 

 About the Faculty   

 The Institute for Intelligent Networked Systems (INSI) at Northeastern University London focuses on advancing next-generation wireless systems and intelligent connectivity. Building on INSI’s global research leadership, the London campus brings together expertise in AI, neuromorphic computing, and wireless communications to explore transformative technologies for 6G and beyond. The institute fosters close collaboration with industry and academia, providing an interdisciplinary environment for innovation, hardware prototyping, and impactful real-world research. 

 The Faculty of Computing, Mathematics, Engineering, and Natural Sciences (CoMENS) is undergoing significant growth at Northeastern University London. It is home to four interdisciplinary undergraduate dual-degree (in UK and US) programmes in the areas of Data Science, Data Science and Politics, Computer Science and Business, and Computer Science and Philosophy; four postgraduate programs in the areas of AI Ethics, Data Science, Computer Science, and Technology Leadership; and five degree apprenticeship programmes in the areas of AI, Data Science, Digital and Technology Solutions, and Biosciences. 

 The faculty plays a major part in Northeastern University’s first-year student mobility program, offering undergraduate courses in Computer and Data Science, Mathematics, Engineering, Physics, Biology, Chemistry and Healthcare, striving to inspire and equip entering students to be outstanding scientists.   

 About the University   

 Founded in 2012, Northeastern University London (formerly known as New College of the Humanities) has established itself as a prestigious higher education institution based in the heart of London. Northeastern University London is part of Northeastern University’s Global Campus Network. Positioned as top ranking in the USA, Northeastern has campuses in Arlington, Boston, Charlotte, Miami, Oakland, San Jose, and Seattle in the USA, and Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

 After becoming part of Northeastern University’s global network in early 2019, the University has undergone a period of rapid growth, having been granted Taught Degree Awarding Powers in February 2020 and moved to a new, state-of-the-art campus in 2021.  

 Northeastern University London offers a vibrant, collegiate community delivering broad and academically rigorous degree programmes, designed to equip graduates with the combination of skills and knowledge that are increasingly desired by organisations, employers, and society. It offers state of the art audio visual technology in its teaching and meeting spaces across the organisation.

About the role

End-to-end learning-based constructions are becoming increasingly popular for communication systems, but what do neural networks actually learn when they are trained to communicate: do they rediscover Shannon-theoretic constructions, or something new? The forward process of a diffusion model is a Gaussian channel, so should a diffusion model be viewed as a joint source–channel decoder? When every block of a communication system is learned, is the bit still the right interface?

We are seeking a postdoctoral researcher to work on these and related questions at the interface between information theory and modern machine learning, as part of a joint NSF–EPSRC project between Imperial College London and Texas A&M University. The aim is to use information theory both as a lens to explain what learned communication systems do and as a guide to designing new ones, from analytically tractable Gaussian models to real data. Potential research directions include, but are not limited to:

Generative models meet information theory: diffusion models viewed through Gaussian channels and estimation, generative priors for communication and compression at extremely low rates, and rate–distortion–perception trade-offs.
Opening the black box of learned codes: what neural encoders learn on tractable (e.g., vector Gaussian) sources, whether they recover known constructions such as Shannon–Kotel’nikov mappings or superposition codes, and what a “neural interface” between source and channel coding should look like.
Multi-user and networked settings: correlated sources over multiple-access and relay channels, and communication-efficient inference and learning with large models at the network edge.

These questions are timely: generative AI is reshaping how data are compressed and transmitted, and AI-native, semantic and task-oriented communication are being considered for 6G, yet principled answers about what learned systems can and cannot achieve remain scarce. You will be encouraged to develop your own research agenda within this space, from fundamental limits to over-the-air demonstrations on our software-defined radio testbed.

This full-time, in-person postdoctoral position is based at Imperial College’s South Kensington Campus in London, UK, and is funded for up to 24 months, starting in January 2027 or as soon as possible thereafter.

The Research Associate will be supervised by Prof. Deniz Gunduz within the Electrical and Electronic Engineering Department at Imperial College London. Co-supervision will be provided by Prof. Krishna Narayanan and Prof. Chao Tian at Texas A&M University (USA), through regular joint meetings and research visits.

What you would be doing

Key responsibilities include: 

To shape and lead your own research agenda within the themes above
To undertake original research of international excellence
To develop fundamental theory and turn it into practical learned coding and communication schemes, validated in simulation and, where appropriate, on our software-defined radio testbed
To write reports for submission to research sponsors
To present findings at international conferences and at joint project meetings with Texas A&M University
To publish in leading venues in information theory, machine learning and communications (e.g., IEEE Trans. IT, ISIT, IEEE JSAC, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR)
To collaborate closely with researchers at Texas A&M University, and to help mentor PhD students

What we are looking for

Education:

Hold a PhD (or be close to completion*) in electrical engineering, computer science, mathematics, statistics, or a related field.

Experience

Practical experience within a research environment and / or a track record of publications at leading venues
Strong expertise in one or more of the following, and a willingness to learn the others:
Information theory (e.g., rate–distortion theory, joint source–channel coding, multi-user information theory).
Coding and communication theory.
Design, implementation and training of deep neural networks, including generative models (e.g., diffusion models, transformers).
Optimisation methods.
Experience with programming in Python and deep learning frameworks (e.g., PyTorch or JAX)
Desirable: prior work on learned compression, neural channel coding, joint source–channel coding, or semantic/task-oriented communication; hands-on experience with diffusion or other generative models; experience with software-defined radio or wireless prototyping.

Knowledge

Knowledge and research experience in one or more of the following areas: information theory, coding theory, communication theory, learning theory, optimisation, and generative models.
Knowledge of research methods and statistical procedures.

Skills and Abilities

Ability to conduct a detailed review of recent literature
Ability to develop and apply new concepts
Creative approach to problem-solving
Excellent verbal communication skills and the ability to deal with a wide range of people
Excellent written communication skills and the ability to write clearly and succinctly for publication

What we can offer you

The opportunity to continue your career at a world-leading institution and be part of our mission to continue science for humanity.
An international collaboration with leading information theorists at Texas A&M University, with regular joint meetings and funded research visits.
Access to GPU computing resources and a software-defined radio testbed for over-the-air experiments, and a dedicated conference travel budget.
Freedom to develop your own research directions, opportunities to co-supervise PhD students, and support for independent fellowship applications (e.g., RAEng, EPSRC).
Grow your career: gain access to Imperial’s sector-leading dedicated career support for researchers as well as opportunities for promotion and progression.
Sector-leading salary and remuneration package (including 39 days off a year and generous pension schemes).

How to apply: please submit a CV with a full publication list, a research statement (max. 2 pages) describing how your expertise relates to the themes above, and up to three representative papers. Visa sponsorship is available for this role.

For any specific queries regarding the post please contact Prof Deniz Gunduz (d.gunduz@imperial.ac.uk)

About the role

How can we design a watermark that survives editing or paraphrasing? What does it mean, information-theoretically, for a model to have `forgotten’ a training example? What is the price in utility of preventing a model from leaking its training data?

We are seeking a postdoctoral researcher to tackle questions like these within INFORMED-AI, the UKRI AI Hub on Information Theory for Distributed AI (Imperial, Bristol, Cambridge, Durham). The aim is to bring the tools of information and coding theory (e.g., hypothesis testing, channel coding with adversaries, rate-distortion theory, and operational measures of information leakage) to enable trustworthiness of modern generative models, and to turn the resulting insights into practical algorithms.

Potential research directions include, but are not limited to: watermarking and provenance for LLMs and diffusion models (fundamental detectability-quality-robustness trade-offs, watermarks that provably resist adversarial editing, and connections to information hiding and arbitrarily varying channels); machine unlearning (information-theoretic definitions and certificates of forgetting, and efficient algorithms that achieve them); and privacy-preserving training and inference (privacy-utility trade-offs, membership inference and memorisation viewed as hypothesis testing, and privacy in federated and distributed learning).

These questions are extremely timely and important: regulation such as the EU AI Act is beginning to require that AI-generated content be watermarked, while principled answers are still missing. You will be encouraged to develop your own research agenda within this space.

About the role

We are recruiting a Research Associate to lead the lung bioelectronics programme within DAPHNE, an ERC Starting Grant that investigates how extracellular matrix deformation and strain-induced electrical polarisation regulate lung immunity, stromal cell behaviour and fibrotic progression. You will develop bioelectronic in vitro platforms that control mechanical deformation and electrical polarisation, then use them with human lung cells to identify mechanisms linking matrix signals to fibrotic cell-state transitions.

The post is based within the National Heart and Lung Institute and will work across bioelectronics, mechanobiology, pulmonary biology and quantitative analysis. The role will combine live-cell and fluorescence lifetime imaging, molecular assays and spatial transcriptomic approaches.

What you would be doing

Design and optimise bioelectronic in vitro platforms built around engineered hydrogels and synthetic extracellular matrix systems with controlled stiffness, deformation, ligand density and electrical polarisation.

Plan and run experiments with human lung fibroblasts, macrophages and epithelial cells in two- and three-dimensional culture, including multicellular disease models.
Measure cell-state transitions using live-cell imaging, FLIM, confocal microscopy, molecular assays, cytokine profiling and spatial transcriptomic or related multi-omic approaches.
Analyse high-dimensional imaging and molecular datasets using statistical methods and, where suitable, AI-assisted image analysis, machine learning or predictive modelling.
Maintain rigorous experimental records, coordinate day-to-day integration across the project and support the scientific development of two PhD researchers.
Prepare publications, funder reports and conference presentations and contribute to further funding applications.

What we are looking for

A PhD, or near completion of a PhD, in bioelectronics, biophysics, tissue engineering, biomedical engineering, mechanobiology, biomaterials, cell biology or a closely related discipline.

Strong practical experience in at least one of extracellular matrix biology, biomaterials, hydrogel systems, three-dimensional culture or disease-relevant cell-matrix models.
Evidence that you can design, build and troubleshoot multi-step in vitro platforms and interpret physical and biological measurements together.
Experience in live-cell or advanced fluorescence imaging, molecular assays or quantitative cell-state analysis.
Experience in analysing high-dimensional imaging or biological datasets; AI-assisted image analysis, machine learning, computational modelling or predictive modelling would be advantageous.
Clear scientific writing, careful data stewardship and the ability to work constructively across disciplinary boundaries.
Experience of pulmonary fibrosis, macrophage-fibroblast biology, spatial transcriptomics, multi-omics, mechanosensitive ion channels, microphysiological systems or student supervision would be advantageous.

What we can offer you

A central scientific role in an ERC-funded programme with direct influence over lung bioelectronic platform design and cross-project integration.

Access to Imperial facilities and collaborators spanning lung biology, biomaterials, microscopy and quantitative analysis.
Dedicated project resources for biomaterials, cell culture, imaging, conference participation and specialist training.
Ten development days each year for research staff, alongside Imperial career support and opportunities to build supervisory and project-leadership experience.
A collaborative and inclusive research environment within the National Heart and Lung Institute.

Further information

This is a full-time post of 35 hours per week. The appointment is fixed term until 30 Jun 2029.

Please note that this is a PhD-level role. A successful candidate who has submitted their thesis but has not yet been formally awarded the PhD will be appointed as a Research Assistant until the award is confirmed.

Through LASE we aim to deliver outstanding education, impactful research, and meaningful regional and global impact.

Do you have the expertise in AI and predictive modelling to help improve how wind turbines operate in icy conditions? If so this role could be ideal.

We’re looking for a Research Associate to join OptimICE, an international Horizon Europe project bringing together 14 organisations to reduce the impact of icing on wind energy in cold climates. This 42-month fixed-term role offers the opportunity to contribute to research that improves how wind turbines are monitored, operated and maintained in icy conditions.

Working with research partners to deliver project objectives and milestones

postings.advert_text:
Research Fellow in Economic Early-warning Signals of Accelerated Climate Change and Earth-System Tipping Points
Overview of the Role

Are you a researcher with demonstrable expertise in the analysis of climatological data and the implementation and interpretation of climate model projections? Do you have a demonstrable interest in engaging with stakeholders, particularly in public policy and the financial sector? Do you have a background within climate science? 

This project will address the lack of adequate early-warning systems for accelerated climate change and tipping-points, for the insurance sector and more broadly. It also aims to address an associated challenge for the insurance sector, given its criticality to the global economy, by helping the sector understand the stressors, and adaptation responses to those stressors, it is likely to face in the coming decades due to the combined effects of climate change, the transition to a net zero economy including regulatory challenges, and potential geopolitical threats.

Through this work, in collaboration with the insurance and reinsurance industry, the successful candidate will help to develop and test a novel early-warning system for accelerating climate change and tipping-points, with aim of informing policy and wider society that unmanageable levels of climate change, with different modalities of climate impacts, are approaching.

This approach draws on ideas from climate attribution and optimal fingerprinting and from economics signal detection but extends this through the application of social science techniques, including decision-gaming and reverse stress testing, by using the insurance sector as a filter to help detect the early signs of an accelerated climate change signal against the background noise of natural variability in the climate.

As part of this early-warning system development, we will produce multi-dimensional storylines using interdisciplinary teams to combine understanding on physical climate change, policy and regulatory changes linked to the net zero transition, and potential geopolitical impacts. These will be applicable to stress-testing in insurance, but with broader applications across finance as well as for government and other sectors aiming to adapt.

The successful candidate will also work closely with collaborators across the University (the Faculties of Business and Environment and Social Sciences) and with co-investigators at the University of Oxford to contribute to the development of cross-cutting underpinning methodological advancements, including new approaches to describing and characterising confidence levels, treatments of uncertainty in bringing together disparate data and models, approaches to characterising compounding and correlated risks, and tail-risk scenarios including tipping points. The candidate will apply these to a range of hazards, which could include sea level, heat waves, drought, flood, and wildfire and will work as part of multi-disciplinary teams to connect science with decision-making approaches relevant to financial institutions. 

Some experience of working with climate model data will be essential for the role and both researchers will work in one of the most cutting-edge areas in climate research with high societal impact. Qualified candidates must demonstrate a commitment to research excellence and impact in the relevant disciplinary field. 

What we offer in return

26 days holiday plus approx.16 Bank Holidays/days that the University is closed by custom (including Christmas) – That’s 42 days a year!
Generous pension scheme plus life assurance– the University contributes 14.5% of salary
Health and Wellbeing: Discounted staff membership options at The Edge, our state-of-the-art Campus gym, with a pool, sauna, climbing wall, cycle circuit, and sports halls.
Personal Development: Access to courses run by our Organisational Development & Professional Learning team.
Access to on-site childcare, shopping discounts and travel schemes are also available.

And much more!

 About Us 

 The Department of Politics and International Relations (DPIR) is one of Oxford’s largest and most internationally recognised departments, home to around 90 academic staff and a thriving community of researchers and visitors. Ranked the Number One University in the UK for Politics by The Guardian in 2024, the department delivers world‑class teaching and research supported by experienced Professional Services teams working across Courses, Research, Finance, HR and Communications. We are committed to equality of opportunity and an inclusive working environment and are proud to hold an Athena Swan Bronze Award. DPIR is based in the Social Sciences Building on Manor Road, alongside Economics, Criminology, Socio-Legal Studies and the Social Science Library.

 About the Role  

 The Teaching and Research Fellow will play a central role in the development, delivery and evaluation of the leadership components of a new cross-Departmental programme, Flourishing Futures.

 The programme, headed by Prof E. J. Milner Gulland in the Department of Biology, seeks to nurture the next generation of leaders with nature as a core concern. It will integrate character and leadership development with opportunities for students to engage with the natural world.

 The postholder will have particular responsibility for the research and development of a framework for character-based leadership for nature, designing and delivering associated character and leadership development activities, and undertaking research to understand and evaluate their impact.

 The Oxford Character Project (OCP) explores how leadership can be a force for good in an increasingly interconnected and rapidly changing world, with a distinctive focus on the role of character. Through conceptual and empirical research, the OCP investigates the importance of character for good leadership and how virtues of character can be effectively cultivated across diverse institutional context.

 About You 

 The successful applicant will design and refine programme content and teaching materials, drawing on the Oxford Character Project’s theoretical and empirical research. You will also manage student programmes by recruiting participants, facilitating workshops, hosting guest speakers, and overseeing events and associated administration.

 In addition, you will undertake collaborative theoretical and empirical research into character and leadership development, and design and conduct quantitative and qualitative studies to gather participant feedback and evaluate programme impact.

 You will hold of be close to be completion of a doctoral degree in the humanities or social sciences relating to character education and leadership development. You will also have a strong track record in character and leadership education, supported by excellent theoretical and empirical knowledge in these fields, and also bring expertise in both quantitative and qualitative research methods suited to studying character and leadership development.

 This position is full-time and fixed-term until 30 September 2028 and available from 1 January 2027. 

 If you have any questions about the role, please contact the DPIR HR Team at vacancies@politics.ox.ac.uk . All enquiries will be treated in strict confidence and will not form part of the selection decision.

The opportunity

The University of the Arts London (UAL) is seeking to appoint a highly motivated Research Fellow on a 10-month fixed-term contract to work on the UKRI AHRC-funded project The Antigravity Machine: Escaping Convergence Through Scaffolding Artistic Plurality in AI, part of the AI Humanities Sandpits (Canada, UK and US). The project brings together researchers at UAL, Simon Fraser University, York University (Toronto) and the University of Dundee with creative practitioners and cultural and industry partners to build open, process-oriented generative AI tools that support exploratory creative practice rather than automating it away.

The Research Fellow will play a central role in delivering the project’s technical development, research, and co-design activities in the UK. Working closely with the Principal Investigator, the co-investigators, and a Canadian Research Fellow counterpart, the Research Fellow will write code for the project’s generative AI software and contribute to applied and practice-based research investigating how artists and designers can navigate the latent space of generative models on their own terms, keeping hold of cultural specificity and resisting the pull of the dominant cultural attractors, or gravity wells, that steer outputs towards generic, majority-culture defaults.

The Research Fellow will be a hands-on member of the technical team building the Antigravity Machine (AGM) software, an open-source, locally deployable system for image and text generation. This will include contributing code to the captioning and training-data pipelines, LoRA adapter fine-tuning, ComfyUI workflows, the interactive latent-space navigation interface, the energy dashboard, and C2PA provenance on outputs. The Research Fellow will also help maintain the open adapter repository, API documentation, and a public-facing website that lets independent artists and small organisations adopt the software without specialist support.

Your profile
The ideal candidate will be a confident programmer with demonstrable experience of working directly with open generative AI models, such as Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Llama, or Mistral: running them locally, fine-tuning them, and building on them in code, rather than only using them through commercial apps or APIs. This includes Python, PyTorch, Hugging Face Diffusers and Transformers, and tools such as ComfyUI.
They will also have experience of collecting and analysing qualitative data such as interviews and focus groups, and of planning and facilitating participatory workshops. They will need excellent organisational skills to coordinate development, data analysis, and reporting across two countries, and awareness of and interest in the challenges and opportunities of working collaboratively across disciplines and time zones. Skills and interests in interface design, web development, and accessible or inclusive interaction design are also desirable. Good spoken and written English language skills are essential to support this international project. 
We are UAL

University of the Arts London (UAL) generates and inspires the creativity the world needs for a better future. Since 1842, our colleges have been defining creative education. With curiosity, imagination and intent we make work which creates lasting change for people and our planet. London is core to who we are, a place where we meet and share ideas with people from different backgrounds and cultures.

Our creative network influences learning, culture, industry and society on a global scale. Our academics and practitioners deliver creative education and inspire new ways of thinking through research and innovation. We work with students at every level from pre-degree and short courses to postgraduate and online learning, enabling them to build the careers they want. Together, we are a community of makers, thinkers, pioneers and storytellers redesigning the future.

As a University, we are ranked second in the world for Art and Design. We are formed of 6 Colleges with unique histories and identities: Camberwell College of Arts, Central Saint Martins, Chelsea College of Arts, London College of Communication, London College of Fashion and Wimbledon College of Arts. UAL also has 4 Institutes, 5 Research Centres, 1 Pre-Degree School and 2 subsidiary companies delivering specialist activities.

We are a global University, welcoming over 22,000 students and 6,000 staff from 130 countries. We aim to be a university where people can be themselves and feel supported to reach their full potential. That’s why we are proud to hold a Bronze Award from the Race Equality Charter (REC), are members of the Business Disability Forum and Employers for Carers, and maintain our status as a Disability Confident Scheme and Living Wage employer.

Application process

We operate a fair and open anonymous selection process. Thus, you will need to create an account and submit an application through our application portal. As part of this, you will need to provide a supporting statement/answer some competency questions to demonstrate your suitability. Our recruitment process involves: Application, Shortlisting, Interview and Assessment, Offer, Onboarding.

We understand the benefits of using AI in work. But, if you are thinking of using it to submit an application, we ask you to think about what value it adds. AI tools tend to lack the personal touch and authenticity we value in candidates. We encourage you to showcase your unique knowledge and skills using your own voice.

If we receive a high volume of applications, the closing day date might close early. We aim to communicate any changes to the closing date with at least 24 hours’ notice. If you have any general questions or have accessibility needs, please refer to our Contact us page.

 About the role  

 Applications are invited for a Postdoctoral Research Associate post in mass photometry and glycobiology to work under the supervision of Professor Weston Struwe. The project, funded by the UKRI, centres on developing advanced methods for quantitative characterisation of glycocalyx-associated interactions, including how viral glycoproteins (e.g. SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1) engage with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). The project focuses on improving the current capability of protein-carbohydrate interaction measurements by mass photometry. Specifically, the work entails recombinant glycoprotein and GAG expression, developing solid supported lipid bilayers and GAG-decorated surfaces. 

 This full-time fixed-term post is funded by the UKRI for up to 8 months in the first instance.

 The actual starting salary offered will be based on qualifications and relevant skills acquired and will also be determined by the funding available.   

 About you  

 You will hold a PhD/DPhil, or be near completion of a PhD/DPhil, in Chemistry, (Bio-)Physics, Biochemistry or a related discipline, with strong knowledge of the relevant research field and experience in mass photometry, glycobiology, supported lipid bilayers, and handling glycosaminoglycans and virus glycoproteins. You will be motivated, enthusiastic and able to work independently and collaboratively, with excellent communication, laboratory record-keeping and organisational skills. You will be willing to develop new mass photometry applications, contribute to laboratory responsibilities, support junior colleagues and participate in international conferences. Experience in mass photometry (MP) instrumentation, glycobiology or carbohydrate chemistry is required, while expertise in MP data analysis, glycan-dependent interactions, glycosaminoglycan purification, viral glycoprotein characterisation and glycan-mimetic surfaces would be advantageous. 

 What We Offer  

 Your happiness and wellbeing at work matters to us, so we offer a range of family-friendly and financial benefits including:

 An excellent contributory pension scheme

 38 days annual leave

 A comprehensive range of childcare services

 Family leave schemes

 Cycle loan scheme

 Membership to a variety of social and sports clubs

 Discounted bus travel and Season Ticket travel loans

 The University also runs a large number of social groups and sports clubs for those looking for more than just a great place to work.

 Application Process 

 Applications for this vacancy are to be made online via the above 'Apply' button and Vacancy ID 189701 . You will be required to upload your curriculum vitae and a supporting statement, setting out how you meet the selection criteria for the post, using examples of your skills and experience. Click here for information and advice on writing an effective Supporting Statement. As part of your application, you will be asked to provide details of two referees and indicate whether we can contact them now. 

 For further details, please refer to the How to apply section of the job description. Any further enquires may be directed to recruitment@bioch.ox.ac.uk .

 The closing date for applications is 12.00 noon on Monday 30 November 2026 . Only applications received before this time can be considered. Interviews for shortlisted candidates to be held as soon as possible thereafter.

 About Us  

 The Department of Politics and International Relations (DPIR) is one of Oxford’s largest and most internationally recognised departments, home to around 90 academic staff and a thriving community of researchers and visitors. Ranked the Number One University in the UK for Politics by The Guardian in 2024, the department delivers world‑class teaching and research supported by experienced Professional Services teams working across Courses, Research, Finance, HR and Communications. We are committed to equality of opportunity and an inclusive working environment and are proud to hold an Athena Swan Bronze Award. DPIR is based in the Social Sciences Building on Manor Road, alongside Economics, Criminology, Socio-Legal Studies and the Social Science Library.

 About the Role  

 The Postdoctoral Research Fellow will work with Prof Petra Schleiter (Principal Investigator) to conduct research for an ESRC funded research project on the effects of voter ID in the UK. The appointee will be part of a research team including co-Is Prof Margit Tavits and Prof Jonathan Homola.

 The project examines the effects on voters’ behaviour and attitudes of the introduction of mandatory photo ID in the UK, where citizens have no national ID cards. It combines (i) original surveys with embedded experiments with the analysis of historical data on the introduction of voter ID in (ii) Northern Ireland in the early 2000s, and (iii) in the English voter ID trials of 2018 and 2019.

 The Postdoctoral Research Fellow will work on all strands of the project, with a particular focus on a new strand of work that focuses on young voters. This strand examines the effects of voter ID requirements on the political participation, attitudes, and experiences of the youngest cohort of voters, including potential future voters in the 16 to 17 year old age bracket. The Postdoctoral Research Fellow will work closely with other members of the team, including the PI and Co-Is.

 About You   

 You will contribute to designing a survey experiment, code and test survey instruments, monitor data collection with the survey firm, and carry out data‑quality checks. Additionally, you will adapt existing and develop new research methods suited to the data, while managing your own research activities and workload with appropriate initiative and judgement.

 Furthermore, you must hold or be close to completion of a doctorate in political science or a related field and have experience of survey experiments, survey design and survey data analysis as well expertise in advanced quantitative methods, research design, and experience of working in R.

Applications are invited for an ERC-funded Postdoctoral Research Associate (Grade 7) or Senior Research Associate (Grade 8) position in cosmology within the Relativity and Gravitation Group of the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics.

While candidates in all areas of cosmology will be considered, candidates interested in collaborating with Professor Blake Sherwin on CMB or large-scale structure cosmology (for example, on areas related in some way to CMB lensing or kSZ science) will be of particular interest. The successful candidate will work with Professor Blake Sherwin as well as academic staff across the Relativity and Gravitation group and the Kavli Institute for Cosmology (www.kicc.cam.ac.uk).

Applicants should have or should soon receive a PhD in a relevant area of physics or astronomy, and have an established track record of original research and experience of working in collaboration.

Duties include developing and conducting individual and collaborative research objectives, proposals, and projects. The role holder will be expected to plan and manage their own research and administration, with guidance if required, and to assist in the preparation of proposals and applications to external bodies. You must be able to communicate material of a technical nature and be able to build internal and external contacts. You may be asked to assist in the supervision of student projects, the development of student research skills, provide instruction, or plan/deliver seminars relating to the research area.

Please see the Further Particulars documents for the full criteria of a Research Associate and Senior Research Associate position. Appointment will be made to either level.

Further information about CTC can be found at www.ctc.cam.ac.uk and the GR Group at www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/research/gr/.

Fixed-term: The funds for this post are available for 3 years in the first instance.

Start date: The intended start date for this position is 01 October 2027 (or by negotiation).

Informal enquiries may be made to LE51639@maths.cam.ac.uk.

Please indicate the contact details, including their email addresses, of three academic referees on the online application form and upload a full CV and a description of your recent research (not to exceed three pages).

Please make your referees aware that they will be contacted by the Mathematics HR Office Administrator to request they upload a reference for you to our Web Recruitment System; and encourage them to do so promptly. Ensure that at least one of your referees is contactable at any time during the selection process. The deadline for reference submissions is 29 December 2026.

 This is your opportunity to join a vibrant community of scholars, receive funding for your research, and make a lasting impact in your field.

 The Notre Dame – St Edmund’s Junior Research Fellowship in Global Catholicism is a three-year, stipendiary postdoctoral position open to early-career scholars who have recently completed a PhD or expect to hold a PhD by the commencement of the Fellowship, in one of the following fields:

 English

 History

 Modern Languages

 Theology

Interdisciplinary proposals are welcome, including proposals that, while retaining an overall humanistic perspective, bring the disciplines listed above into dialogue with the social sciences.

 Join us for three years as a Junior Research Fellow

 Pursue your work in English, History, History of Art, Modern Languages, Philosophy, or Theology

 Networking with global experts and fellows

 Access to research resources

 Opportunities to develop and present your work

 Career development workshops and seminars

 Engagement in an active interdisciplinary community

About the role

Bacterial infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in humans. Innate immune cells are essential for detecting bacterial pathogens and generating anti-bacterial immunity. We strive to decipher the processes that regulate anti-bacterial immune responses, and the mechanisms through which bacterial pathogens evade or manipulate the immune responses.

We are seeking a forward-thinking, passionate and ambitious Postdoctoral Research Associate to explore the functional consequences of bacterial pathogen interactions with human inhibitory receptors. This post is funded by an Wellcome Trust grant awarded to Dr Alex McCarthy, which aims to provide fundamental insights into the role of inhibitory leukocyte immunoglobulin like receptors (LILRs) in bacterial infections. This will be achieved by utilising microbiological, cellular and in vivo infection models.

What you would be doing

You will be performing cutting edge research combining molecular, microbiological, cellular and in vivo infection-based approaches to contribute to an advanced understanding of invasive bacterial diseases. You will be based in the group of Dr Alex McCarthy in the Centre for Bacterial Resistance Biology (CBRB), and in the Section of Molecular Microbiology within the Department of Infectious Diseases (DoID) at Imperial College London. Your research will address questions on the functional properties of inhibitory receptors, their capacity to regulate anti-bacterial immune responses and their role in bacterial infection biology.

You will be expected to take a lead in planning and designing the studies (with support from the PI). You will take initiative in the planning of research. You will have clear and timely communication with the Group leader and work closely with researchers within the group. As part of your development, you will attend and actively contribute to relevant workshops, lab meetings, research seminars and conferences in Imperial and the wider community. You will supervise both undergraduate and postgraduate research students.

What we are looking for

We are looking for a highly motivated candidate with research interests in bacterial infection biology. Applicants must demonstrate as part of their application, how they meet the essential criteria required of the post.

You will

hold a PhD in bacterial infection biology or host-pathogen interactions, or a closely related area.
have experience of performing research using techniques relevant to bacteriology, host-pathogen interactions and/or bacterial infection biology.
have experience in a broad range of molecular biology, biochemical and/or cell biology techniques.
possess excellent verbal and written communication skills.
have published your research in relevant and refereed journals.
enjoy working on your own initiative and collaboratively. 
form positive relationships with the research group and wider community.

What we can offer you

The opportunity to contribute to innovation in bacterial infection biology.
Training in complementary aspects of bacterial infection biology in the Centre for Bacterial Resistance Biology.
The opportunity to collaborate with other researchers and PhD students in the Group of Dr Alex McCarthy.
The opportunity to continue your career at a world-leading institution and be part of our mission to continue science for humanity.
Grow your career: gain access to Imperial’s sector-leading dedicated career support for researchers as well as opportunities for promotion and progression.
As a member of research staff you have 10 development days to use to develop your skills and explore your career prospects
Sector-leading salary and remuneration package (including 43 days off a year and generous pension schemes).
Be part of a diverse, inclusive and collaborative work culture with various staff networks and resources to support your personal and professional wellbeing.

Further information

More information on

research in the McCarthy laboratory here.
on the Centre for Bacterial Resistance Biology is here.
on the Department of Infectious Diseases is here.

This role is for a fixed-term contract for 24 months. You will be expected to work 100% of your time on-site

If you require any further details about the role, please contact: Alex McCarthy (a.mccarthy@imeprial.ac.uk). Please note that this email address is for enquiries only and you should not send your application to this email. CV and covering letter should be submitted via the online application as detailed below.

Please note that this is a PhD level role but candidates who have not yet been officially awarded will be appointed as a Research Assistant.

*Candidates who have not yet been officially awarded their PhD will be appointed as a Research Assistant within the salary range £45,399 - £48,876 per annum.

 We are looking for an enthusiastic and capable Research Fellow to join our School of Health at Leeds Beckett University, on a full-time, fixed-term basis of approximately two years (February 2027 to February 2029), at Grade 7. The post-holder will lead the day-to-day delivery of a systems-informed process evaluation of the Childhood Obesity Prevention Initiative (COPI), an international, multi-city programme funded by Novo Nordisk. This is a highly applied and predominantly qualitative role, working at the forefront of applied systems science in public health and, uniquely, with international partners. We are therefore looking for someone who combines strong qualitative research skills with a genuine interest in how complex public health programmes work in practice.

 Our ‘School of Health’ offers a wide portfolio of professional courses and research in health and social care. For more information see www.leedsbeckett.ac.uk/school-of-health 

 Ours is a friendly and supportive place to work. You will join a collegiate research team with an established track record in systems-informed evaluation of complex public health interventions, working alongside the Principal Investigator (Dr James Nobles) and co-investigators, who are keen to share expertise and provide mentorship. Structured development and training are available from our ‘People and Organisational Development’ team and the ‘Centre for Learning & Teaching’.

 Expectations and benefits 

 The successful candidate will hold a PhD (awarded, or due to be awarded imminently) in a relevant discipline and will bring demonstrable experience of qualitative research methods and an understanding of the complexity of public health and public health interventions. Experience of systems-informed evaluation methods, of facilitating workshops or participatory research, and of international or cross-cultural research would be an advantage. The post involves some international travel, though this will not be a significant part of the role. 

 A full list of essential and desirable criteria is set out in the candidate pack. Please provide clear evidence in your application of how you meet each of the essential criteria. These criteria form the basis on which applications are assessed and will be explored in detail at interview.

 For an informal discussion, please contact the Principal Investigator, Dr. James Nobles j.d.nobles@leedsbeckett.ac.uk .

 Closing date: Monday 30th November 2026 (23:59)

 We welcome applications from all individuals and particularly from black and minority ethnic candidates as members of these groups are currently under-represented at this level of post. All appointments will be based on merit.

 Leeds Beckett University is a Disability Confident Employer. Disabled candidates who demonstrate all essential criteria within the Person Specification will be invited to an interview.

 In this role you will lead on the development of materials, catalysts, electrochemical characterisation, electrochemical modelling and corrosion performance evaluation within the remit of the Horizon Europe Project ‘REUSE’ (RP12W61135).

 This is an exciting post where you will work closely with Dr Paul and Dr Maniam to develop novel catalysts for electroreduction of CO2. To model the electrochemical and corrosion behaviour, multi-physics models will be developed and evaluated. The Project will ultimately develop a technology demonstrator prototype of the electroreduction of CO2.

 The University of Oxford is a stimulating work environment, which enjoys an international reputation as a world-class centre of excellence. Our research plays a key role in tackling many global challenges, from reducing our carbon emissions to developing vaccines during a pandemic.

 The Nuffield Department of Orthopaedics, Rheumatology and Musculoskeletal Sciences (NDORMS) is part of the Medical Sciences Division and is the largest European academic department in its field, running a globally competitive programme of research and teaching. The Kennedy Institute is a biomedical research centre uniquely bringing together discovery science and early-stage clinical research, to develop transformative new therapies for chronic inflammatory and musculoskeletal conditions.

 What We Offer 

 As an employer, we genuinely care about our employees’ wellbeing and this is reflected in the range of benefits that we offer including: 

 •               An excellent contributory pension scheme 

 •               38 days annual leave 

 •               A comprehensive range of childcare services 

 •               Family leave schemes 

 •               Cycle loan scheme 

 •               Discounted bus travel and Season Ticket travel loans 

 •               Membership to a variety of social and sports clubs 

 About the Role 

 In this role you will establish and optimise SPI-LLSM experiments to investigate molecular binding and diffusion in model membranes that mimic immune cell membranes, and subsequently extend these measurements to live immune cells. You will use and maintain the ZEISS LLS7 lattice light-sheet microscope at the Oxford ZEISS Centre of Excellence and the PicoQuant Luminosa microscope at the Rosalind Franklin Institute. You will be responsible for selecting, implementing and adapting experimental protocols for preparing model membranes, performing reaction–diffusion assays and bioconjugation reactions, and conducting SPI-LLSM measurements. You will also design experiments to benchmark and validate the technology.

 About You 

 You will hold a Bachelor’s Degree (or Master’s) in physical chemistry, pharmacology, biophsyics, chemical biology. You will have practical experience in quantitative fluorescence spectroscopy and microscopy, including fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS), relevant to establishing SPI-LLSM measurements in model membranes and live cells. You will possess sufficient specialist knowledge of molecular spectroscopy, fluorescence photophysics, fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM), Fluorescence Lifetime Correlation Spectroscopy (FLCS) and molecular diffusion to contribute to established research programmes investigating protein membrane interactions and reaction–diffusion processes. Experience in the quantitative analysis of fluorescence or imaging data using custom written MATLAB, Python routines is essential. Experience in glycochemistry or site-specific installation of post-translational modifications on proteins is desirable.

 Applications are invited for a Realist Researcher in the Primary Care Workforce and Learning research group led by Professor Sophie Park ( https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/research/groups-and-centres/workforce-and-learning-research-group ). The GAP LEAP project includes a realist review, evaluation, appreciative inquiry and co-production of a toolbox to support additional healthcare professional learning in general practice. It is funded by the NIHR HSDR programme. The project aims to understand the nature of additional healthcare professional (AdHCP) workplace-based learning (WPBL) in the general practice setting and how this might be enhanced and strengthened. In particular, the project explores how the undifferentiated and complex nature of patient needs can be well supported in this setting. The project uses a realist approach to produce a review, appreciative inquiry, toolbox co-production and evaluation. The findings will inform the design of future policies, interventions, and support systems to help general practice approaches to inter-disciplinary workplace-based learning (e.g. education approaches, supervision) to maximise equitable patient care.

 The successful applicant will join a multi-disciplinary and multi-institutional team with expertise in primary healthcare organisation and design, workforce sustainability, realist evidence synthesis, qualitative research, and co-production. They will be involved in completing the realist review, translating programme theory development into other work packages and elements of the project. They will work in collaboration with PPI and stakeholder colleagues throughout the project, including co-production of the toolbox. They will lead submission of an NHS ethics application for the evaluation empirical work package. They will conduct observation + analysis for the empirical evaluation work package in collaboration with Exeter and Newcastle Research Fellows and the wider research team.

 The successful applicant will be supported in their career development including presentation at suitable conferences and written publications. Applicants will also be encouraged to participate in departmental activities including some teaching and citizenship activities as agreed with their line manager.

 You will have a doctoral degree (e.g. PhD/DPhil) in a relevant subject (e.g. public health, primary care, health psychology, sociology, epidemiology, evidence synthesis, or equivalent), with post-qualification research experience, and possess sufficient specialist knowledge in the discipline (workforce, primary care, continuity, general practice sustainability) and approach (realist and qualitative methods) to inform research and develop future research projects and methodologies.

Research Fellow in Health Sciences/Psychology Ref: 44423 (Fixed Term)
Location
Brighton, UK
Hours
Full-time considered up to a maximum of 1.0 FTE (37.5 hours) Requests for flexible working options will be considered (subject to business need).
Salary
Grade 7 starting at £39,560 to £46,970 per annum, pro rata if part time.
Contract Type
Fixed Term Contract
As part of our recruitment approach, internal candidates will receive priority consideration at the shortlisting stage.

About the role

Applications are invited for a Research Fellow to join the Sussex Health Outcomes Research and Education in Cancer (SHORE-C) unit within BSMS, based at the University of Sussex for a fixed-term position of 24 months at 1.0 FTE. SHORE-C is an internationally recognised research centre with particular expertise in patient reported outcomes. The team work on a variety of clinical trials and observational studies, develop and evaluate supportive interventions, develop information and education materials for patients and their families and provide communication skills training.  You will be working on the Living With Metastatic Breast Cancer project (LIMBER3). LIMBER3 is a qualitative study using community-based participatory research methods to co-produce resources for people with secondary breast cancer and guidance for health care professionals. There may also be opportunities to contribute to other SHORE-C projects. 

About you

You will have a PhD (or equivalent experience) in a relevant discipline such as health psychology, nursing, medicine or an allied health profession. You will be skilled in research methods including interviewing and qualitative analysis and be able to communicate complex findings clearly to a range of audiences. You will have a track record of delivering Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement activities. We are looking for someone who is organised, proactive and collaborative, with excellent problem-solving skills and the ability to manage competing priorities. A developing publication record and enthusiasm for contributing to funding applications, teaching activities and wider research impact would be advantageous as would familiarity with participatory research methods.

About our School

Brighton and Sussex Medical School (BSMS) is an equal partnership between the Universities of Sussex and Brighton together with NHS organisations throughout the South-East Region. BSMS is committed to inclusivity, sustainability, medical education in a multi-professional context, and promoting the highest possible standards in our teaching, clinical practice and research (ranging from early translational to applied).

Working together, our Academics, Technicians and Professional Services staff co-ordinate the passionate delivery of teaching and research, allowing us to remain one of the leading choices of medical schools in the UK. Our staff are multiskilled and work across varied teams, which are diverse, experienced and dedicated. 

Our object as a School is to strive for excellence in education, training and research allowing us to support all in a constantly changing healthcare sector. We work to create a nurturing and supportive environment in which our staff and our students can succeed and thrive.

Our medical research has developed a strong reputation for making a real impact locally, nationally and internationally.

Ultimately, our research aims to:

•           improve medical treatment

•           answer fundamental biomedical and clinical questions

•           deliver more personalised healthcare to patients.

Please find further information regarding the School at Brighton and Sussex Medical School.
 
Brighton and Sussex Medical School is proud to hold a Gold Athena Swann Award.

Why work here

Our university is situated off the A27, next to the beautiful South Downs where you will enjoy everything that our 150-acre campus has to offer. We are accessible by public transport; Falmer train station is a five-minute walk to campus and several bus stops are located within campus. We also have dedicated cycling paths and encourage our staff to use these with our offering of a cycle to work scheme.  

Sussex is a renowned, multi-accredited, research-led International University and this is only possible because of the people that work here. Whether you are a member of Faculty, part of a Professional Services team or a Student, it’s our people that make us great and we want you to be part of that. 

Find out more about our reward and benefits package. 

Find out about our equality, diversity and inclusion. 

Further Key Information 

Please contact Valerie Shilling at v.m.shilling@sussex.ac.uk or 01273 873019 for informal enquiries.

The University of Sussex values the diversity of its staff and students, and we welcome applicants from all backgrounds.

Eligibility

Visa Sponsorship Queries: This role may be eligible for sponsorship under the Skilled Worker route. The assigned SOC code is 2119 Natural and social science professionals not elsewhere classified and the going rate is £41,500. Eligibility for sponsorship will depend on the salary offered, whether a candidate can make use of tradeable points to meet the salary offered, or whether the candidate holds an existing Skilled Worker sponsorship which began before 4 April 2024.

The University requires that work undertaken for the University is performed in the UK.
